chapters.summary: Chair Mercedes Narcisse convenes the oversight hearing on H&H's NYC Care program and access to health care for uninsured New Yorkers. She frames the hearing around the program's role in the city's health care safety net.
chapters.title: Chair Narcisse opens oversight hearing on NYC Care and uninsured New Yorkers

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I am Council Member Mercedes Narcisse, Chair of the Committee on Hospitals.

chapters.summary: Narcisse notes New York State's low uninsured rate achieved through Medicaid, the Essential Plan, and Child Health Plus, but says access remains uneven. She cites a 2025 DOHMH report finding immigrant adults nearly twice as likely as U.S.-born adults to be uninsured.
chapters.title: Narcisse outlines state coverage gains and persistent disparities

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us today for our oversight hearing on examining H&H NYC Care Program and access to health care for uninsured New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Over the years, New York State has made significant progress in expanding access to health insurance and today has one of the lowest uninsured rate in the nation.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Through investment in Medicaid, the Essential Plan, Child Health Plus, and other public coverage programs, millions of New Yorkers have gained access to preventive care,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: primary care providers, prescription medications, and treatment for chronic conditions.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yet, despite these achievements, access to coverage remains uneven.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Certain populations, including immigrants, or our new arrival,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Hispanic New Yorkers and Black, and many working families continue to experience higher rates of uninsurance and face barriers to enrollment.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: In maintaining coverage.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: In New York City, a 2025 report from the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene found that immigrant adults were nearly twice as likely as U.S.-born adults to be uninsured.

chapters.summary: Narcisse describes NYC Care, launched in 2019 as a Bronx pilot under Mayor de Blasio and since expanded citywide. The program offers low- and no-cost primary care, specialty care, behavioral health, OB/GYN, dental, eye care, and durable medical equipment regardless of insurance, income, or immigration status.
chapters.title: Narcisse describes NYC Care's launch and covered services

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: For New Yorkers who fall through the cracks of the traditional insurance system, New York City Care by NYC Health Hospitals serve as a critical part of the city's health care safety net.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Established under Mayor Bill de Blasio, the program launched in 2019 as a pilot.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: at H&H facilities in the Bronx and has since expanded citywide,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: providing uninsured New Yorkers with low-cost and no-cost health care services regardless of insurance, income, or immigration status, including primary care,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: specialty care services like cardiology, rheumatology, orthopedics, and podiatry.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Mental health and substance abuse services, referrals to specialists like social workers, therapists, and psychiatrists,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: obstetrics and gynecology, family planning, STI testing and treatment, affordable medications,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: eye care, dental care, emergency services, and other social support services, and access to durable medical equipment, which is DME by most,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: to eligible New Yorker care patients.

chapters.summary: Narcisse says federal eligibility cuts caused about 197,000 New Yorkers to lose coverage, citing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's cuts to New York's Essential Plan. She warns that new Medicaid eligibility requirements taking effect January 1, 2027 could affect as many as 900,000 New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Narcisse details federal cuts and projected coverage losses

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: However, border cuts to health care eligibility at the federal level have caused approximately 197,000 New Yorkers to lose coverage.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Get that number, 197,000 New Yorkers to lose coverage.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: In July of 2025, President Trump signed

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, H.R.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: 1, which included cuts to federal funding for New York's essential plan.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Beyond the essential plan reduction,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: HR1 also imposed new Medicaid eligibility requirements that are expected to take effect on January 1st, 2027.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: City officials estimate that as many as 900,000 New Yorkers could be affected by that federal Medicaid changes, which is one big ugly bill for us.

chapters.summary: Narcisse lists ongoing barriers to enrollment and retention, including complex eligibility rules, renewal requirements, language barriers, unstable employment, and housing insecurity. She says these disruptions lead residents to delay or skip care.
chapters.title: Narcisse lists barriers that disrupt coverage and care

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Beside the recent federal policy changes,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: There are several other ongoing barriers that prevent eligible city residents from enrolling in or maintaining health insurance coverage.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Challenges such as navigating complex eligibility rules, renewal requirements, language barriers, limited familiarity with the health care system,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: unstable employment, lack of employer-sponsored insurance, housing insecurity, and difficulties accessing enrollment assistance often lead to coverage disruption.

chapters.summary: Narcisse warns that uninsured New Yorkers often seek care only after conditions worsen, increasing emergency department demand and uncompensated care. She says this strains safety net hospitals that already serve disproportionate shares of Medicaid and uninsured patients.
chapters.title: Narcisse warns of emergency department strain from uninsurance

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Disruptions in care can have detrimental consequences.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Uninsured individuals are more likely to delay or skip medication and treatment because of cost concerns, leading to higher risk of chronic diseases and early mortality.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: As a result, New Yorkers may seek care only after their conditions have become more severe.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Increasing demand for emergency department services and uncompensated care, which could place additional financial and operational strain on New York City's safety net hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Which already serve a disproportionate share of Medicaid and uninsured patients.

chapters.summary: Narcisse argues preventive care is cost-effective, calling inaction 'penny-wise, dollar-foolish,' and cites last week's ambulance response time hearing. She thanks committee counsel Raina Lee, policy analyst Manoa Butt, financial analyst Molly Howard, and her staff before turning to the oath.
chapters.title: Narcisse on preventive care investment and thanks committee staff

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Preventive care plays a critical role in keeping New Yorkers healthy and reducing the need for costly emergency interventions.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We call it penny-wise, dollar-foolish.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Last week, during the committee's joint hearing in ambulance response times, we heard firsthand about the significant strain already facing the city's emergency department and EMS workforce.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Ensuring that residents can enroll in and maintain health coverage is an important part of addressing these challenges.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: as access to preventive and primary care can help reduce our vulnerable emergency room visits and ease pressure on the broader health care system.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Continued investment in programs that support enrollment and re-enrollment in health care coverage will be essential to strengthening New York City's health care safety net.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: As New York faces a period of uncertainty in health care coverage,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Understanding how New York City Care is serving uninsured residents and how the city can strengthen its healthcare safety net will be more important than ever.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I look forward to today's testimony.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I know the room is not as crowded as expected because this is a big deal.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Testimonies will help us, right?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Today we'll be hearing from stakeholders and shareholders, of course, opportunity to expand awareness of the program and any policy.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Operational or outreach investment that may be needed to ensure New York City care continues to meet the evolving needs of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Before I conclude, I would like to thank Committee Counsel Raina Lee, Policy Analyst Manoa Butt, Financial Analyst Molly Howard, and my staff for all the work they do.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: especially in the district office.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I want to say thanks to Deputy Chief Frank Shea, Drashina Jailo, and of course, my dear fellow, that's Matthew Lee.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you for being here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I would like to turn it over to the committee council to administer the oath witness from the administration.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Raina?

chapters.summary: Dr. Ted Long, H&H system chief medical officer, introduces himself and NYC Care Executive Director Dr. Jonathan Jimenez. He says NYC Care has received national recognition for its impact on health equity and frames H&H's mission amid federal changes.
chapters.title: Dr. Ted Long introduces H&H team and NYC Care's national recognition

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: My name is Dr.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Ted Long.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I'm a primary care doctor in the Bronx and our system chief medical officer for clinical services and population health at New York City Health and Hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairwoman Narcisse and members of the Committee on Hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I am joined today by Dr.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Jonathan Jimenez, Executive Director of NYC Care and a family physician at New York City Health and Hospitals, Gotham Health, Cumberland.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's exciting for me to share with you today why NYC Care has received national recognition for its impact on health equity and the impact this program has had on New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: At New York City Health and Hospitals, our focus is on being a fully integrated health system that enables New Yorkers to live their healthiest lives.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: As we see healthcare access changing rapidly due to shifts at the national level with the implementation of HR1,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: H&H is committed to excellence in healthcare, innovating to increase awareness of the importance of preventive healthcare while making it as affordable and accessible as possible for New Yorkers typically excluded.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: This is where NYC Care enters.

chapters.summary: Long recounts NYC Care's 2019 Bronx launch and 2020 citywide expansion, describing it as the nation's largest initiative guaranteeing care regardless of immigration status or ability to pay. He says the program has about 125,000 members and outlines eligibility and enrollment channels including 646-NYC-CARE.
chapters.title: Long on NYC Care's launch, eligibility, and enrollment channels

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: In 2019, NYC Care launched in the Bronx before expanding to all five boroughs in 2020

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: with the goal of bringing a healthcare access membership program that guarantees low-cost and no-cost services to New Yorkers who do not qualify or cannot afford health insurance based on federal guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: This program is the nation's largest and most comprehensive.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: comprehensive initiative to guarantee health care regardless of immigration status or ability to pay, and brings direct access to New York City Health and Hospitals, the nation's largest public health care system.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Today, NYC Care has approximately 125,000 members.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: An individual is considered eligible if they do not qualify for or otherwise cannot afford private health insurance based on federal income guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: To learn more about their eligibility and get enrolled, New Yorkers can meet with a New York City Health and Hospitals financial counselor, visit one of our 20 community-based organizations, or call

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: the NYC Call Center at 646-NYC-CARE.

chapters.summary: Long details covered services on a sliding fee scale at 11 hospitals and Gotham health centers, noting no premiums, deductibles, or co-pays. He highlights a two-week primary care appointment offer, a 24-7 multilingual hotline, prescription benefits, and a new durable medical equipment benefit used by over 2,500 members.
chapters.title: Long details NYC Care services, sliding scale, and member supports

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Once enrolled, NYC Care members can access covered services on a sliding fee scale at our facilities, which includes our 11 hospitals and all of our Gotham Community Health Centers.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Since NYC Care is not health insurance, there are no premiums, deductibles, or co-pays.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: New patients are offered a primary care appointment within two weeks at one of our health and hospitals locations.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: NYC Care members gain access not only to primary care and preventive care services, but the full slate of specialty care that health and hospitals offers.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: This includes routine screenings, mammograms, and services such as obstetrics and gynecologic care,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: dental care, behavioral health care, and eye care.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Members can have visits with any provider within our network.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Within behavioral health care, services include mental health and substance use treatment, as well as access to telehealth and virtual express care.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Members have access to a 24-7 member service hotline in over 300 languages and dialects by calling the same NYC Care number that they may have used to enroll.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Members also have access to affordable prescription benefits and 24-7 pharmacy access.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: As of 2025,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: NYC Care members also have access to low-cost or no-cost prescribed DME or durable medical equipment for their medical conditions, a benefit that over 2,500 members have utilized during its first year.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Accessing high-quality, affordable health care services that put patients first should not be a challenge, and NYC Care aims to make it as seamless as possible.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: NYC Care meets New Yorkers where they are to bring exceptional health care services to all.

chapters.summary: Long says NYC Care has logged over 1 million community outreach interactions and 1 million primary care appointments. He cites peer-reviewed studies showing NYC Care members achieve comparable primary care use and chronic disease control to new Medicaid enrollees.
chapters.title: Long on outreach, primary care appointments, and peer-reviewed outcomes

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Since its launch, NYC Care has had over 1 million community outreach interactions in collaboration with contracted CBOs throughout the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Additionally, NYC Care members have completed over 1 million primary care appointments.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Peer-reviewed studies have shown that new NYC Care members and new Medicaid enrollees show comparable utilization of primary care and specialty care.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: More importantly, the two groups show the same level of chronic disease control.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Above all, Health and Hospitals is focused on keeping New Yorkers engaged in preventive health services, which not only has positive impacts on New Yorkers' long-term health, but also for H&H.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Data shows that even when members become eligible for health insurance and can disenroll from NYC care, they stay engaged in care at H&H.

chapters.summary: Long describes H&H's primary care growth, including over 70,000 new primary care patients and a panel size increase from 1,500 to 1,750 patients per provider. He credits expanded care teams, data-driven scheduling, and reduced no-shows.
chapters.title: Long on primary care growth, panel sizes, and care team model

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Over the last five years, New York City Health and Hospitals has seen substantial growth in primary care, with over 70,000 new primary care patients.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Today, New York City Health and Hospitals has more patients in primary care than in the history of our system.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: This has been made possible through initiatives including

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: expanding primary care physicians'abilities to see more patients, allowing for more new patient access, increasing from 1,500 patients per full-time provider to 1,750.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Adding to our staffing model to ensure that primary care physicians seeing more patients does not impact access to timely care,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: which means increasing the care team so that patients can get their care inside and outside the clinic from team members that include their primary care doctor, advanced practitioners that work directly with their doctors, chronic disease nurses.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Chronic disease clinical pharmacists, social workers, and community health workers.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Using timed, data-driven clinic slot opening tools to ensure the highest utilization possible for primary care providers has also increased access.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Finally, focusing on reducing no-shows through an iterative process so that no appointments go unused, including

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: changes to the SMS and telephone call reminder systems, both the messaging itself as well as the timing of the messaging.

chapters.summary: Long closes by saying H&H's North Star is treating health care as a human right, and that NYC Care delivers real, comprehensive care with meaningful equity results. He thanks the committee and offers to answer questions.
chapters.title: Long closes testimony: health care as a human right

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: At New York City Health and Hospitals, our North Star is to treat healthcare as a human right and provide the highest standard of care to all who walk through our doors.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: NYC Care continues to provide access to real, comprehensive healthcare that shows meaningful results in advancing healthcare equity for its members.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Rooted in innovation, patient trust, and an overarching goal to ensure all New Yorkers, regardless of their immigration status or ability to pay, have access to health care, NYC will keep making health care a human right in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today on this incredibly important topic, and I'm very happy to answer any questions.

chapters.summary: Narcisse acknowledges attending members and asks how many New Yorkers are currently enrolled in NYC Care. Long answers 125,766 as of October 23.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks how many New Yorkers are enrolled in NYC Care

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Before I go any further, I want to acknowledge you've been joined by CM Fedler, Powers, Albert, Albert, or I'm just always missing out on that one.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And who else?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We started since I have a member from the union and Shirley always said, right.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Health care is a human right, and you just said it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That's right, because when you're in New York City specifically, since we're the lead city, I believe they call us capital of the world, so we need to do that effectively, especially when it comes to health care.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And we were having that discussion here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Healthcare, without your health, you're nothing, basically.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So healthcare is so important for us to keep it going and giving folks, you know, care.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That's what we are here for.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So how many New Yorkers are currently enrolled in NYC Care?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So our current number, this is as of October 23rd when we pulled the data, 125,766.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Say it again, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I just got distracted for a minute.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I talk at great speeds.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks how enrollment has changed since 2019 and whether recent Medicaid and Essential Plan changes increased enrollment. Long recounts his first NYC Care patient who hadn't seen a doctor in 43 years, says the program exceeded its 100,000 goal and peaked near 150,000, and attributes the decline to patients transitioning to Medicaid.
chapters.title: Long recounts NYC Care enrollment growth and decline since 2019

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How has New York City Care enrollment changed since its launch in 2019?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And has the program experienced increased enrollment following recent changes to Medicaid and Essential Care, Essential Plan?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for asking.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So going back to 2019, because my team and I were the same team, we launched the program in 2019.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So I remember every detail of it.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And I'll tell you a quick anecdote about the first patient that I ever saw with NYC Care and talk about how that's contributed to the numbers increasing over time and some of the changes.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: What NYC Care really did starting in 2019 is it unlocked healthcare access in a way that people didn't believe that they had it before.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: My first patient was a woman that hadn't seen a doctor in 43 years.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Never had a mammogram, never had a pap smear, didn't know if she had diabetes.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I gave her everything, all the preventive care that she deserved in that visit.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I'm careful to use the word deserved because at the end of it, she started crying and I asked her why and she said,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: before seeing me and enrolling in the NYC Care program, she'd never felt like she deserved, that was her word, care before.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It was heartbreaking, but it really stuck with me that that's the difference that we made in her life, and then I have no doubt she went and told 10 friends and family members, and within the first couple years of the program, we blew through our initial goal.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We initially set out to enroll 100,000 New Yorkers in the NYC Care program.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We blew through that, reached up to about 150,000 at the height of the program.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And since then, with today we're having 125,000.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The reason for us losing about 25,000 patients, the main reason is not a bad thing.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: New York State, in the context of the program, has allowed for people that are 65 and above to enroll in Medicaid if they're low income, regardless of immigration status.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we actually were able to have a lot of our NYC care patients that I know transition from being NYC care to New York State Medicaid.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But the good news is they're still at New York City Health and Hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That's a good one, to have people able to go to Medicaid.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But now, with the re-enrollment, it will be a problem for more folks to transition from NYC care to Medicaid for what's going on right now and the central plan.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I truly believe in the work that you're doing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We have been joined by...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Farias, Amanda, on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So thank you for that, for having someone in New York City seeing a doctor after 43 years.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So that's been the work we're doing with NYC Care is so important.

chapters.summary: Narcisse cites the Mayor's Management Report showing NYC Care enrollment decreased in fiscal 2026 and asks what factors drove the decline and what strategies H&H is using. Long explains the shift to Medicaid for seniors 65 and older regardless of immigration status.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about fiscal 2026 enrollment decline and outreach strategy

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: According to the mayor's management report, NYC Care enrollment decreased in fiscal 2026, which we just spoke about.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What factors contributed to the decline?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You told me that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So what is the report?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What strategy that you're doing to bring?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: New one?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Like, if we're still promoting, what are we doing?

chapters.summary: Long says NYC Care has always prioritized community engagement through 20 contracted CBO partners and offers appointments within 14 days. He warns that 'coverage disruption' will define the coming period, with recertification and work requirements creating temporary gaps that NYC Care must catch.
chapters.title: Long on CBO outreach and preparing for coverage disruption

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yeah, so right now, just to zoom out for a second, NYC Care, since 2019, has always sought to do as much community engagement as we can.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It says that every New Yorker knows that health care is their human right if they enroll in this program, and we welcome everybody through our doors.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: An important way we do that, by the way, is that we offer an appointment to you within 14 days of your phone call.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So if you call us, we're going to offer you maybe an appointment near to where you live, maybe a few blocks down the road, but always within 14 days.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So in terms of to your question about how we've sought to increase or grow the program, I would say we've continued to work with our 20 contracted CBO partners to continue to get the word out about the program and then enroll you in the program

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: if you're not eligible for health insurance and then make you that appointment within 14 days.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: One important point I just want to draw out, because I'll quote you from earlier,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Turn this east because it's resonated with me.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Coverage disruption is going to be the name of the game going forward here.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's not like people are just going to fall off of Medicaid and just enroll in NYC care and that's problem solved.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: People are going to have changes in eligibility.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: There's a recertification piece that's going to change.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Work requirements, they may not get their certification in time and then have to submit later, so they may be temporarily in NYC care.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So what we want to do is we want to, today, make sure that everybody knows not only is this program a place where you can go treat health care as a human right in our city, but if you fall off of health insurance, the program will catch you.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So that's a transition that we're making in the messaging that we're working through our community-based organizations to do.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And we expect that, especially with these changes coming up associated with not only the EP5 changes, which I can go into more detail about, but the upcoming Medicaid changes, predominantly recertification and work requirements, we're going to need to catch more people than ever.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So now our goal is to get as ready as possible so that every New Yorker can always know that health care is a human right through the NYC Care Program.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks H&H to walk through the NYC Care enrollment process and identify operational barriers. Long begins by stressing that enrollment starts with screening for insurance eligibility.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks H&H to walk through NYC Care enrollment process and barriers

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And can H&H walk us through the NYC care enrollment process and identify any operational barriers that may prevent eligible New Yorkers from successfully enrolling?

chapters.summary: Long explains that every enrollee goes through financial counseling, and those ineligible due to immigration status or affordability can enroll by phone via MyChart, in person, or through CBO partners. He notes lack of phone or internet access as a barrier and cites DOH form 5090 for self-attestation of identity.
chapters.title: Long explains three enrollment pathways and financial counseling

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yeah, it's a really good question, and I'll answer it.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: There's three specific ways you can enroll.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Before I go to that, I want to make an important point.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The enrollment process for NYC Care starts, before I go into the details, with seeing if you're eligible for insurance.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: If you're eligible.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: If you're eligible for insurance, we want to enroll you in insurance.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: If you're eligible for Medicaid, we want to enroll you in Medicaid.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's better for you and better for our system, better for our city.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So the first step of enrollment is every single NYC Care enrollee has to go through what we call financial counseling, or in other words, to see if they're eligible for health insurance.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: For those that aren't eligible, which will happen for two reasons, the first reason being based on immigration status, the second reason being if it would cost you too much money based on federal

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: guidelines to be able to reasonably afford health insurance, then we would offer to enroll you in the NYC Care program.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And there's three ways that that happens.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The first is we could do it actually all over the phone now.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we would talk to you on the phone.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We could register you in MyChart, which is like a portal you get on your phone, and you can actually upload the documents that I need you to upload through MyChart.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So it's a fairly seamless process that way.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: A barrier that we've seen there, to answer your question about barriers, is if you don't have a phone or internet access, that would be a barrier to using that phone-based option because it does rely on you giving us the documents.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: In that case, we transitioned to option two, which is in-person enrollment.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So you can come and enroll in person, even if you've been evaluated for health insurance by the phone, or you can do the whole thing in person.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So I have patients that are coming in to see me for the first time.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: They'll go through the whole insurance eligibility process and then either end up with an insurance plan or NYC care in the context of seeing me.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The third way you can enroll is through one of our trusted partners, one of our community.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: based organizations.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: They go through a similar process.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So you'll be evaluated for health insurance, and if you aren't eligible for health insurance, they can enroll you in the program.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And there's certain forms that they ask you for that they can help you to upload.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I'll give you an example here of one of the forms.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So there's the DOH form 5090, which is your self-attestation of identity if you don't have the standard forms.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we work with you based on where you are to make sure that if you have the standard forms or if you don't, you can fill out that form to have you upload the right documents so we can enroll you in the program quickly.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks how H&H promotes the program to uninsured patients who come to a hospital. Jimenez says H&H will never turn anyone away and will figure out insurance applications in parallel, and Long urges everyone to remember 646-NYC-CARE.
chapters.title: Narcisse and Jimenez on enrolling uninsured patients at hospitals

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So my follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So if someone come in a hospital, they don't have any insurance at all.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So right there, they can be assessed right there.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: They don't have.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So how do we promote for folks to just come and find out?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Like, where are you at?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Yeah, as Dr.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Long said, the goal is to connect every single New Yorker to health care.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And we want to make sure that if they're eligible for insurance, we enroll them.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And so that's the first step.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: But it's not a barrier.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: We always tell people in the community, our community organizations, anyone that we get in touch with, come to us.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: If you need care, we will not turn you away.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: We will take care of you no matter what, no matter your immigration status or your income.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And we'll figure out the process of applying for health insurance at the same time in parallel.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: These pathways are for people who are having the forethought, they're planning, right, they're calling, they already know they want a primary care appointment.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Well, we can start that process.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: As they have those documents available.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So basically, if you call on the phone, you want to be seen by a doctor, so their role, or whoever received calls, however, is to come in, we'll care for you, and we'll find out whatever else.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And in fact, when you call our call center, before you complete the process of enrollment, they ask you,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: where and when you would like to make your primary care appointment.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Because the point is, can we get folks connected to primary care?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Every single New Yorker, that's the goal.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So if you remember one thing from Dr.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Jimenez and me today is, however many numbers it is, 10 numbers.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: 646-NYC-CARE is the one number to remember, the one number you can share with everybody.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's the one-stop shop for everything we're going to talk about today.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Six foot.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You can repeat it again for people watching to know that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: 646-NYC-CARE.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay, we're promoting it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We have been joined by CM Sanchez.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks how long enrollment takes from first contact to activation. Long says it takes 30-45 minutes with documents in hand, with materials mailed in about two days to a week, and stresses that an appointment is offered immediately.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks how long enrollment takes; Long details timeline and member card

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How long does the enrollment process typically take from initial contact to activation of service?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: If you have your documents with you, we can go through that process in 30 to 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Once you submit them to us, it can take, you know, I think it's two days to a week or so for you to get in the mail the stuff that we're going to send you, which is really important.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I'll actually come back to that in a second.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But I think what Dr.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Jimenez is saying is very important that even as we're enrolling you in the program and we're going to be sending you things in the mail, we're going to make you that appointment right away.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: That's what's the most important thing.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And we're really proud, and I just really want to underline this because it was so hard to do.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We've offered more than 90% of all NYC care enrollees since 2019 an appointment within two weeks.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Which is unheard of across the rest of the country or on the private side.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Call another health care provider and try to get a new patient appointment in two weeks.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's nearly impossible.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we're very, very proud that we've moved heaven and earth.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We literally had Saturday meetings running the list of those that we didn't have a two-week appointment for and calling them back and offering them a sooner appointment just to make sure.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: sure they could feel what it meant to really access health care through the program.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: To go back for a second, when we said we mail you things in the mail, this is very important.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So before the NYC Care Program, we would never turn anybody away from New York City Health and Hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But your experience was you'd call and we'd say, sure, we'd love to see you, but the wait time can be three months, six months.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And then you may take that appointment, and then you may find access somewhere else, and you may not end up going.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we had a very high no-show rate, but we were scheduling people really far out, so it wasn't as meaningful to them.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: What we're doing now, and you didn't know who your doctor was going to be.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So when you enroll in the program now, we send you a card, a member card in the mail that will have your name on it, your doctor's name on it.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The 24-7 contact number to call, 646-NYC-CARE, with any questions you have about anything.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And then also your individualized fee scale.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So you, for example, chair and our C's would know this is how much it's going to cost to see Dr.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Long.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: This is how much each medication is going to cost me based on my individualized income because we got all that data for you when we were evaluating you for health insurance.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: This is how much it's going to cost to see every specialist.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's how much it's going to cost to go to the emergency room.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So all those financial barriers that existed yesterday before the program are all torn down today to give people that certainty of being able to access care without financial fear.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We also are going to mail you a brochure, which has all the information in it with what it means to be part of the program.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We want to make you feel like you're a part of something, a part of the program.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And I think that's one of the secret ingredients that's kept people coming back and made the program so effective.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Oh, I'm going to have to follow up on that.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks how the specialty referral process works after enrollment. Long explains the e-consult system, where primary care doctors send questions to specialists who triage urgency, and says about one in five patients gets an answer without needing an appointment.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about specialty referrals; Long explains e-consult triage

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Specialty.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Let's say they come from another doctor and they know specifically what's wrong.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And to see a specialty.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And after their enrollment, how long you be, let's say a GI or cardiologist, how the process goes.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Great question.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So this is something that yesterday the answer probably would have been simpler before the program existed where you just would have a referral and you'd get into the queue.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We've completely changed that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So the way it typically works now is if you

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: get seen somewhere else, let's say you go to the emergency room and you're told to come to the health and hospital, something like that, you'll come through the front door of primary care.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So I see patients all the time that were referred from a specialist outside the system or went to the emergency department or had an admission and then were referred to us.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I will then see them, evaluate them, and what we do for specialty care now, which is way more effective than the system we had before, is we have something called e-consult.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So basically, let's use an example.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: If you're having a racing heartbeat or something, I can ask that question via e-consult to the cardiologist.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And the cardiologist, so you're not just going to get put into a queue regardless of being triaged.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: They're going to actually triage and say, okay, I would like to see this patient in seven days, in three days, in 14 days, in 30 days.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So the specialist is already having a role in triage before your appointment's even booked.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: That makes it so that if you have more of an urgent issue, we'll get you in more quickly, and the specialists are involved from day one after that referral is placed.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: A lot of times, too, what happens is...

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: You may have been referred to us.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I'll give another example here.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: A patient, this was a long time ago, with a mass in their wrist.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I got the x-ray.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: There was a concern.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The read of the x-ray was concerning for a potential, you know, it was listed as a growth.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Growth can mean cancer.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: That's very scary.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But I sent the e-consult, and the patient wasn't even triaged to be seen.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It was just answered, oh, it's normal.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So the patient didn't even have to worry about seeing ortho.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So e-consult not only gives us, and statistically it's about one out of every five.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: patients gets the answer within a matter of hours from the specialist so that they don't even have to wait for the appointment.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But everybody else gets their specialty appointments based on the urgency that's defined by the specialist that will be seeing them.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: I'll add to that briefly, just that the point, I think, for our patients and for all New Yorkers is just get their problem taken care of, wherever it is, whether it's a cardiologist or a primary care doctor.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And what's happening now is I feel well supported as a family doctor.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: I have all the specialist's knowledge at my fingertips to take care of that problem right there and then where the patient is.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: I think usually when patients are asking for a cardiologist or an ENT, they think they need that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: To get the problem taken care of, but often a primary care doctor can do it with the right support, and that's what we're doing right now.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I agree.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks what percentage of applicants complete enrollment and the most common reasons they don't. Jimenez says 90% of uninsured patients have gone through insurance screening, and cites missing documents and need for extra support as barriers.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks what share of applicants complete enrollment; Jimenez on barriers

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What percentage of individuals who begin the enrollment process successfully completed, and what are the most common reasons applicants do not ultimately enroll?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Do you have a percentage?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: We don't have the percentage, but we know that many folks complete the process of enrollment because our goal is that,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: I think actually, sorry, I recall right now we have 90% of our uninsured

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: patients have gone through the process of health insurance screening.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: So they either have health insurance or they're enrolled in NYC care.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: The people who don't, there are many different barriers that go into that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Maybe they're looking for documents they couldn't find.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And it's a process of engagement where we're reaching out to folks.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Every time they come to an appointment, we remind them and encourage them to get in touch with our financial counselors who are well-trained to guide people through that process.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And it's also...

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Importantly for I think this 10% of folks who haven't gone through the health insurance screening process to get enrolled in either insurance or NYC care is some folks need that extra support.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And we also rely on our community-based organizations to walk people through the process to make sure they feel the reassurance that we're there to take care of them no matter what.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And this is just a matter of making sure they get all the benefits that they are entitled to or eligible for.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks what resources or operational changes would ease enrollment. Long and Jimenez emphasize CBO partnerships and direct enrollment by organizations already doing insurance screening, and Narcisse offers the Council and churches as partners.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks what would ease enrollment; Long and Jimenez on CBOs

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What resources or operational changes could help make enrollment easier and more accessible for eligible New Yorkers?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I'll start and I'll see if Jonathan agrees.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I think he will.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The CBOs are a crucial part here.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: You know, if we waited for people to only come to us, I think the program would not have, you know, grown to nearly the size that it is today, which we're proud of.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So I think having trusted messengers go out there into our communities, which has been a cornerstone of the program since 2019, continuing and amplifying that effort, I think especially now when we're entering.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: in a time of confusion with all the changes will be more critical than ever.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We'll do our best to tell our patients what's going on.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We're going to do a ton of outreach to patients as well.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I have some statistics on that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But ultimately, I think a lot of this will fall to the trusted messengers that our patients are going to go to first, the CBOs.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we have to keep those relationships, those partnerships, I think now stronger than ever.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You want to add something?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And I would add that one of the greatest things we've done with our community-based organizations who are already doing health insurance screening is that they're able to directly enroll into NYC Care.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And so expanding those partnerships with organizations, institutions that are already doing the health insurance screening process, which is, as we highlighted, I think the major part of enrollment into NYC Care and Connection.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Would really help us.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: So that's something we're actively always looking for, more partnerships to directly enroll folks into NYC here.

chapters.summary: Narcisse offers the 51 Council members and churches as outreach partners, noting many uninsured residents may be reached through houses of worship. Jimenez and Long welcome invitations to constituent-facing events and ask members to share their communities' needs.
chapters.title: Narcisse offers Council and churches as outreach partners

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I think we can be a source of partnership, 51 of us, and as well as the churches.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We know that when you go to church, you get people.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So on Sunday morning or Saturday, we can get more.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So keep on promoting it throughout because most of the folks that we will find uninsured, a lot of them may end up in churches that you're not going to see on the street or other places.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: I'm glad you mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: We'd love to be at every single event that you all have.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Constituent facing because agreed we never know when we're going to encounter someone

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: who doesn't have a primary care doctor.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And it may be even a friend of someone who doesn't have a primary care doctor, but finding out about NYC Care is crucial, and we want to be everywhere that we can.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And to make that offer concrete, if there are events or places where you think we should go, you know your community is better than we do.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Let us know.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We have teams and community-based organizations that we talked about that we can have go to the events to talk to people, to enroll people.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So I think, again, now people are in more questions than ever.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Given everything going on with Medicaid.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So use us.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We want to be there with you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That's the reason I'm talking about it like this, because I know with whatever going on in the city of New York from the federal, we're paying the price in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So we have to be very smart around it and trying to get our brothers and sisters, the new arrivals out there, help them out.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And we see, I mean, we lived it from COVID that diseases, infectious diseases is not in a bubble.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It can spread to every one of us and we all can be affected.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So the more we align with that, knowing that we're all in it together, the better we'll do.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Definitely.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks what percentage of members receive a primary care visit within six months. Long reiterates that more than 90% of members have been offered a new-patient primary care appointment within two weeks.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks what share of members get primary care within six months

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: After enrolling in New York City Care, what percentage of members receive a primary care visit within six months?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Now, I think some of them you said you're doing excellent on that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Yes, to say it again.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Too excellent.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Because we've worked very hard on this.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: No, you don't have to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because if you want.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay, what do you want to add to it?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: More than 90% of all NYC Care members have been offered a primary care appointment for a new patient appointment within two weeks.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Two weeks.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Two weeks.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That I remember.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Not six months.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks which services NYC Care members use most. Long lists OB/GYN, eye care, dental, cardiology, and podiatry behind primary care, and discusses GI care and colon cancer screening.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks which services NYC Care members use most; Long lists top five

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What services are most frequently utilized by New York City Care members, including primary care, specialty care, behavioral health services, prescription medications, and preventive care?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So the top five that go behind primary care, which is the gateway to everything.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The gateway, okay.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: OBGYN, eye care.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: OBGYN?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: OBGYN, eye care, dental care, cardiology care, and podiatry care.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Not bad.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What happened to the GI?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because we know we have an increase in colon cancer.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That's why I'm saying it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm not saying it has a joke because there's so many people under.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: If we could stay there for a second, it's actually a really good question we think a lot about.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So it used to be that GI was one of the services where there was a bottleneck because we were following what we call the USPSTF preventive services guidelines where you need a colonoscopy every 10 years.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: What we do today, though, which is way more efficient and effective, is we could do an annual test where you don't have to drink the liquid, get put to sleep, go through the colonoscopy, and just do what's called a fit test.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And I talk to my patients about this when I'm in clinic every week.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: All they have to do is just do a quick test once a year, and that's in lieu of.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: of a colonoscopy.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But what that does is, they would have otherwise been waiting in the queue to see a gastroenterologist to get the colonoscopy.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So by doing things differently with the technology that's being developed out there, we've been able to save our gastroenterologists, lowering their wait times for things that really need to go to them, and we're able to do more in primary care.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And patients prefer this so much more.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: You don't have to miss a day of work.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: You don't have to get someone to take care of you that day.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: It's way better, and it's increased our screening rates.

chapters.summary: Narcisse questions why GI isn't among the top services given rising colon cancer rates. Long explains H&H now uses annual FIT tests instead of routine colonoscopies, reserving colonoscopies for patients with abnormal tests or family history.
chapters.title: Narcisse and Long debate colonoscopy versus FIT test

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I will agree and not agree too much on that because the fact is the nurse now going to be not against the doctor, but I will say that

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: for a person that have history, I will definitely let them go on their colonoscopy.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I think it's more.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So we on the same page on that?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: If you have an abnormal test in the past or a strong family history, you do need to still get your colonoscopy.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: For people that don't fall into those two categories, you're eligible for this new test, which fortunately is many people.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And just to also agree with you, one of the things that I'm proudest of that has enabled all of this to work is we have, I think, one of the best primary care staffing models with ratios for all of the nurses who we can't do anything without that are embedded in each of our primary care teams across our whole system.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We could not do hardly anything we've talked about if we didn't have the right team members.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We all work together.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I love that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Jimenez shares that three-quarters of members complete a primary care visit within a year and 80% complete a specialty visit. He notes members also access cardiology, gastroenterology, and orthopedic surgery.
chapters.title: Jimenez shares member primary and specialty visit completion rates

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And I wanted to highlight just a really impressive stat as well that

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Three-quarters of our members complete a primary care employment within a year, and 80% of our members complete a specialty visit within a year.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: So those are just the top five, but they see cardiology, gastroenterology, orthopedic surgery, all of our specialties.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Give me one second.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Now I will pass it on to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: She has to run for books, powers.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how many of the 242,000 New Yorkers who lost Essential Plan coverage are eligible for NYC Care, whether data is available by borough, and how H&H is responding. She also asks how many H&H Medicaid patients will face work requirements starting January 1.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers questions H&H on EP5 losses and Medicaid work requirements

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you so much because, you know, the kids got to get picked up from school.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But thank you for the testimony.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Just really quickly.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I have a question.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I have two questions focused on HR1 and losing essential plan coverage, and I have two on budget and capacity.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'll read all of those questions, and you tell me what I need to repeat.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Sounds good.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Deal?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Deal.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So about 450,000 New Yorkers lost essential plan coverage in July, and only about 242,000 found new plans.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Do we know how many of those 242,000 without plans are eligible for New York City care?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Is this data available by borough?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And how has the health and hospital scene come in, whether by enrolling New York City care or showing up uninsured in the emergency room?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Just over two months from now, how many health and hospital Medicaid patients will be subject to those requirements?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And what will H&H do to support those people?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
