chapters.summary: Long explains that EP5 ended July 1 and, per a September report, about 59% of former EP5 enrollees found another insurance plan, with thousands enrolling in NYC Care. He says the concerted outreach effort offers lessons for the coming Medicaid transition.
chapters.title: Long on EP5 transition and 60% finding new coverage

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I got the three here.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So the first is a very interesting one.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Just to rewind for everybody, EP5 went away on July 1st of this summer.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Among the statistic you're referencing, I believe, was in an article in Cranes from September 4th,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: where it was found that 59% of people that had been in EP5, this is using New York State data, had enrolled in a different insurance plan since July 1st.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So one thing I want to say is there was an open question when EP5 went away.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Nobody knew whether 0% of people were going to find another insurance plan, 100% where that number would fall.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And the answer, at least as of September 4th, was around 60% of people that had been on EP5 had found another insurance plan.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So not NYC care, but another insurance plan.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Many of them went into a different EP category, one, two, three, or four.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Many of them went into Medicaid because based on a change of their income.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And thousands of them on the level of thousands went into NYC care.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But what we've seen is, to me, the conclusion here is that we had a very concerted effort at New York City Health and Hospitals for our patients that

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: had the coverage through EP5 to talk to them right away, early and often, and try to see what they'd be eligible for, another insurance plan or things.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: things like that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So the fact that we, with our efforts and the efforts of others, we're able to help six out of every 10 people in just the first two months alone enroll in another insurance plan shows us that if

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: we can do a good job with a very hard, very concerted effort to close communication with all of our patients,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: to be in touch with them and to make sure that they can stay on an insurance plan.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Is that going to work for everybody?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But this gave us a lot of clues about what doing a good job is and how we can get ready for the Medicaid transition.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: That was your third question.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Maybe I'll skip to your third question.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I'll go back to your second one.

chapters.summary: Long details H&H's preparation for January 1 Medicaid changes, including six-month recertification and work requirements. He says recertification dates are flagged in red in the electronic medical record, financial counselors call patients repeatedly, and nearly 400,000 emails have been sent.
chapters.title: Long on Medicaid recertification and work requirement preparation

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So what are we doing to get ready for on January 1st when the Medicaid changes happen?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: They're going to come in two.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: There's two big components.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: You have to recertify every six months, and you have new work requirements.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we see this coming from, this will be a crisis, don't get me wrong, but we see this crisis coming from a mile away, and we're going to move heaven and earth to do as much preparation as we can, just like we did with EP5.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So for recertification first, today, when I go to my clinic in the Bronx,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: even before recertification on the six-month interval happens, we label it in our electronic medical record.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Your name will come up, and you'll be labeled in red, recertification date of X.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So then I know as your doctor, hey, I want to remind you to talk to one of our financial counselors.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Also, our financial counselors are going to call you many, many times to let you know that your recertification date is coming up.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And here we're going to work with you on it.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Here's what we're going to do to help you.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Here's how we're going to help you to recertify.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we're going to have a very, you know,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: cohesive effort on that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And just to get to stay ahead of that too, here's another statistic.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: To let patients know about what's happening, because we know there's going to be a lot of confusion, we've already sent out nearly 400,000 emails where the message of the email is, if you have questions, call our financial counselor, here's the direct number.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And more than half of them were open.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we're trying to get the word out now.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Our financial counselors are going to serve a really key role.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And from the recertification perspective, all of our team members are going to be aware.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's labeled in red in our electronic medical record.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And we're going to be calling you as often as we can to help you to recertify.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's going to be very hard, but we are going to do everything we can to help.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: On the work requirements piece, there's going to be a lot of questions about this too.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So our financial counselors are going to be our one-stop shop.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: One number to call, the person to talk to is a financial counselor, whether it's about how do you recertify, what documents do you need, what reminders do you need, and also for work requirements, what qualifies as that, what's a certified, you know,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: What are the certified ways to meet the work requirements?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The buzzer.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So on.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I'll finish up on this one.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's very complicated, and I wanted to give you the full picture.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So all of that's to say on the issue of how we're going to help people to enroll in Medicaid, we're thinking about this mechanically and putting very comprehensive plans together with one of the cornerstones being financial counselors and connecting all of our patients to them from our doctors to the emails we send.

chapters.summary: Long says primary care and emergency departments will be the first areas affected by coverage disruptions, with patients worried about losing their doctor turning to the ED. He says H&H is staffing up and monitoring numbers closely.
chapters.title: Long on emergency department impact and staffing up

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Your third question, which I'll just answer briefly, is more of a follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: You asked about the effect on the ED and what we're going to see with the ED as these changes happen.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The first two areas of health care that are going to be affected by this magnitude of, I'll quote Sharon Arcecian, coverage disruptions are going to be primary care.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: People are going to be worried about losing their doctor.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And the ED, people are then going to go to the emergency department.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So our ED colleagues are very aware of this, and we have laser focus on looking at the numbers to see any changes that we see, both in primary care and the ED.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And we're going to be getting ready.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We're staffing up, making sure our teams are ready, aware, so we are prepared.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The chair is going to be gracious to ask my last two questions because I have to hop on the train.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But thank you, chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: My pleasure.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I might as well go to my colleagues there because they have seen next.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks how much NYC Care treatment is delivered remotely and what share of patients requesting remote care don't receive it. He notes lower-income patients with multiple jobs face time constraints.
chapters.title: Epstein asks how much NYC Care treatment is remote

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Can I just ask you about how much of this treatment is remote?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Is remote.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We can pull data on the proportion there of telehealth.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's not a very big number.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, it'd be great to know.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And what percentage of people request remote treatment?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: and aren't getting that kind of remote treatment?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Because we've heard from people, obviously because of family and work, as we said with our colleague, child care, the time that they need to be able to get to medical appointments is really limited, especially people who are lower income who have multiple jobs.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm wondering what H&H is doing to make sure that people have access to remote care.

chapters.summary: Long says he offers every patient the choice of in-person or telehealth visits and that one or two patients per clinic prefer to follow up from work. He notes H&H completed about a million telehealth visits coming out of COVID.
chapters.title: Long on offering telehealth and one million virtual visits

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Well, I mean, on that one, I can give you a much more clear answer.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So, I mean, I live this every week in clinic.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So whenever my patients are being brought back to the clinic, I offer them, do you want to see me in person?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Or I literally say exactly what you just said.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I know you've worked.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I know what your job is.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Do you want to just talk by phone or talk on your phone?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And, yeah, I'd say probably every clinic, one or two of my patients would prefer to follow up from work.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I can see their work in the background and to have a telehealth visit with me.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It used to be more, especially as Chair Narcisse was saying, coming out of COVID, we completed about a million telehealth visits.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we actually, the jury was out a little bit about how people were going to prefer to get care.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And it's turned out to be, we can pull the exact statistics.

chapters.summary: Epstein requests telehealth data broken down by geography to see trends for the NYC Care population and identify barriers. Long agrees to provide the data.
chapters.title: Epstein requests telehealth data by geography

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I would love that data just to be helpful for us to be able to see what that trend is, if more people are doing it.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And if you have it by geographic, you know, like my colleague in the Bronx or my colleague in Brooklyn, we'd love to see kind of what that looks like and whether there's geographic trends for this population and if they're seeking more telehealth or if they're not.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And then figuring out what kind of what those barriers are to wanting it or having access to it.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yeah, totally.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Just to, again, to say from my perspective, we offer it to everybody.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's people's choice whether they want to take us up on that or whether they want to come in to see us.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And what oftentimes happens is so much of what we do requires a test.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So if you need to have your blood drawn or you need to have a mammogram or pap smear or something like that, I think from my patient's point of view, that's one of the reasons why they prefer to just even take time off work to come in to see me.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Because our model of care at New York City Health and Hospitals, which is very important to us, is a one-stop shop.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks how much NYC Care enrollment happens through the SHOW program and how H&H partners with it. Long notes he helped start SHOW in 2021 and that it is expanding 50% this year.
chapters.title: Epstein asks about SHOW program enrollment

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, no, I really do appreciate it, but it would be great if you could follow up with that data.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I would love to figure out how you do enrollment through the show program, like how much of enrollment in New York Cares happens through show and how you would partner with them to ensure that enrollment happens.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So by way of background, my team and I also started the show program in the spring of 2021.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, I know we talked about it back at Bellevue back in the day when it started.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We're still here.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And actually this year we're expanding the show program by 50% in terms of the units we have out every day.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So actually, do you want to take that about show and NYC Care Enrollment?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: I think I actually have to follow up with you.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: So as we discussed, financial counseling and the health insurance screening process is the crux of enrollment in 10YC care or health insurance.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And I don't know if as a part of the show vehicles, they include a financial counselor.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Certainly, telephonically, as we already talked about, they could be connecting folks.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And I know that's a part of.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: all of our processes.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: So I'm almost certain that they're doing that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: But the issue might be about whether they have someone in person.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, I would love to know why they're doing it.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And if they're not, why they're not doing it.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: That might be helpful for us to have that information.

chapters.summary: Long explains that the SHOW program serves unsheltered New Yorkers, most of whom already have Medicaid because they are three times more likely to visit the emergency room. He promises to follow up on specifics of how SHOW enrolls people.
chapters.title: Long on SHOW program and insurance status of unsheltered New Yorkers

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yeah, I can shed a little more light on it.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we'll get back to you about the specifics.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But with the show program, one of the interesting dynamics is the show program is for people experiencing unsheltered homelessness that are living on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And the show program, when we see people, we do have them see if they're eligible for insurance, if they have insurance.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Interestingly, the majority of people that we see that are unsheltered have insurance.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The majority have Medicaid.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: For the reason that, unfortunately, if you're unhoused, you're three times more likely to go to the emergency room.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we see you on that end, and if we enroll you in Medicaid at that point, when you're seeing the show program, you're already enrolled.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So I would view it as, we'll get back to you on the specifics of how show enrolls people.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I think it's by the phone.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We'll get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But the show program is part of a larger ecosystem where we have several different opportunities to enroll people in insurance.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And I would say for better or worse, we do find that most people are already insured.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I appreciate that follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And I know you mentioned that we could help advertise.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: If your team could send over, like, languages we could add to our e-blast, that would be really helpful.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So we would have it that we can just continue to kind of remind people that it's available, you know, especially as Council Member Sylvia Pook's prowess raised.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You know, we're talking about...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: potentially increase in uninsured New Yorkers because of, you know, draconian federal cuts.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So it would be great to have that information we can be sharing out publicly.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We 1,000% agree.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We'll send you everything you need.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And the offer is still on the table for us to join you at any important events from your perspective.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And at the buzzer, I'll say again, I'm going to keep saying this, 646-NYC-CARE.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Chair, can I get just one more minute?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks what New York City's uninsured population was before July 1, 2026, what it is today, and what H&H expects in early 2027. Jimenez cites a DOHMH estimate that up to 900,000 people could become uninsured at the full effect of HR1.
chapters.title: Epstein asks about uninsured population before and after July 2026

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So can you tell us what the New York City unenrolled population was before July 1, 2026, and what the unenrolled population is today?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And what do you expect the unenrolled population will be in January, February of next year?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: You mean the uninsured population?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, sorry, uninsured population.

chapters.summary: Long estimates about 700,000 New Yorkers are uninsured and explains that EP5 ended entirely on July 1, so the 60% figure reflects how many found another plan. He says Medicaid changes will have a similar but different flavor.
chapters.title: Jimenez and Long on uninsured estimates and HR1 impact

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Do you know the numbers?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: The Department of Health and Mental Hygiene recently had an estimate that at the full effects of HR1, there would be close to 900,000 people that might become uninsured.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: But we know, as Dr.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Long was talking about, that many of those folks will find other pathways to connect to health insurance.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And we're certainly going to do everything we can to connect people before they...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, as you said, 60% is likely to be insured in another way.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What is what your experience has been this summer that potentially leaves 40% of almost a million people potentially needing New York City Cares to be able to get some support?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Actually, yeah, let me, to back up for a second, if you'll give me just a minute, I'll try to be as concise as I can with the numbers.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The Department of Health collects the data, so we're not the arbiter of that data.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But for the purpose of this hearing, let's ballpark it.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I think it's 700,000 or so of people in New York City are uninsured.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So a portion of them are part of the NYC Care Program.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And when EP5 went away, EP5 went away in totality.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So everybody that had EP5 on June 30th did not have EP5 on July 1.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So in that scenario, the 60% is of those that lost everything, how many were able to find a different insurance plan?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So it's a related question.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: To me, it's more of how we were able to engage with them to help them to find another plan that they were eligible for.

chapters.summary: Long says Medicaid eligibility isn't changing, but six-month recertification and work requirements will cause many to fall off coverage. He says H&H is terrified but preparing, and that the loss of coverage will be gradual rather than a single-day event.
chapters.title: Long on Medicaid changes and readiness

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: With the Medicaid changes,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's going to have a similar flavor, but it's going to be slightly different.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: People's eligibility for Medicaid is not what's changing.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: They have to recertify every six months, and they have to complete the work requirements.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So it's all of these things that are being put in front of them to ultimately cause a lot of them to fall off of health insurance, which is deeply disturbing to my patients.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I will tell you we're terrified about what's coming up.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But our approach to that is going to be similar.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: That's where there's the strand of similarity with EP5.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We're going to have our financial counselors call you.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We've already sent out hundreds of thousands of communications.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We're going to be in touch with you about the work requirements, helping you to find a program, helping you to understand what a certified requirement is.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: For the with the Medicaid changes, it's not like on January 1, 2027, there's going to be 900,000 uninsured people in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's going to be gradual over time.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So there's two, I would say, equally important things that we have to do to get ready.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Number one, we need to be in touch with our patients to make sure we're helping them to recertify, helping them to meet the work requirement.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And number two,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: For anybody that falls out or loses coverage and falls, NYC cares to be there and be strong and be ready to catch them.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I know that's what we're here for today, but I just wanted to make the point that these things are connected together.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks for a geographic map of NYC Care members and where newly uninsured residents are expected to be, so the Council can target outreach. Long agrees to provide a map and coordinate with the Department of Health.
chapters.title: Epstein asks for geographic map of NYC Care members

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And just one last question.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Just this overlapping map of where you have people through NYC Care.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It's like maybe a geographic map of where those people are.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Are and then where the expectations of people who are losing care are going to be coming from across the city so we can figure out where

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: collectively we can push our resources to ensure, you know, whether in Councilman Rottaball's district or my district, you know,

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: in Councilman Feldman's district, where are we seeing the potential expansion of uninsured people that we can help you get the word out to probably get people to get the care they need to do the prevention.

chapters.summary: Long commits to sending telehealth data broken down per 100 primary care visits and to pulling a map of NYC Care distribution by geography. He says projections of where people lose care may require DOHMH but offers to liaise.
chapters.title: Long commits to telehealth data and NYC Care map

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We'd love that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So just to be concrete about it, I'm a very boring mechanical thinker.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we're going to send you the telehealth data, breaking down for 100 primary care visits, how many are telehealth versus in-person, to help to calibrate about meeting people where they are.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And then we can pull together a map of NYC care distributed by geography.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And then potential data where you think people might be losing care over the next six months where we might want to increase outreach and education.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yeah, on that one, that may be more for the Department of Health.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But we're happy to coordinate, liaise, and ultimately just agree with what you said.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Wherever you are hearing concerns in your community, that's where we want to be.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, if the Department of Health can help you, if you need us to reach out to them directly, I'm sure you have connections to the Department of Health as well.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Sounds like a plan.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But for now, we don't want to know where they are.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: No, you can send it to us.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Sounds good.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I mean, it's...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We know we're going to have issue in New York City and all over the country.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks what percentage of NYC Care members remain actively connected to care one year after enrollment. Long begins to answer.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks what share of members stay connected after one year

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What percentage of New York City care members remain actively connected to care one year after enrollment?

chapters.summary: Long says 77% of members return for another primary care visit after one year and about 80% have had a specialty visit, with 70-plus percent recertifying annually. He explains annual recertification checks whether members have become eligible for insurance.
chapters.title: Long on retention and recertification rates

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So Jonathan shared the numbers, but we can look at this in two different ways.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I think the numbers he shared are probably good ones.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So after one year, 77% come back for another primary care visit.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And I think it's 80% have had a specialty visit in their first year.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: On a continual basis, let's say 70-plus percent recertify with us every year.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We do require you as part of the program to recertify every year.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The reason for that is your income can change or your eligibility for insurance can change.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And if should from year one to year two, you qualify for health insurance, we want to check in with you and be able to get you the health insurance you qualify for at that point.

chapters.summary: Jimenez stresses the message that patients won't lose access to care regardless of insurance status, which he says is critical as people cycle on and off Medicaid. Long shares a patient's fear of losing her doctor after an insurance change.
chapters.title: Jimenez on message that patients won't lose access to care

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: An important message that we deliver to all our patients also as a part of this health insurance screenings process is that you're not going to lose access to care, right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: So we're always telling our patients just come to seek our care regardless of your insurance status.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And this is going to be really important as folks are falling on and off with these new Medicaid requirements and both work requirements and recertification.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I'm assuming they get contact after the recruiting.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I heard that you're saying that you continue correspondence with them, sending them information so they know, despite what's going on now, you still can come to us.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We are here for you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And just to give you another quick anecdote, because that just really stuck with me.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: This is a really scary time.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And people, while they don't understand all the nuance of all the Medicaid changes and all that, people know that scary things are on their horizon.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: They could lose the care that they have.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But from my patient's point of view, I'll tell a quick story.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I had a patient that I saw in clinic recently, and this is heartbreaking.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I worked with her very closely for a serious chronic condition she has.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And I went into my office, and she was there.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: She started crying.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And I asked her what was wrong.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And she said, nothing to do with her health care.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: She said that she had to change an insurance plan because of everything we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And the new insurance plan said that I wasn't the doctor on the plan.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And then she thought she lost me.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And it was terrifying for her.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And I just know that she's just the first of so many people that are going to have that same, you know, fear and really, you know, horrible experience of being told they're losing their doctor, being scared of losing their doctor.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So what we say, what I told her and what I tell all my patients, which is what we tell everybody at H&H, if you lose your health insurance plan, you will not lose your doctor.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And that's what.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: means to treat health care as a human right at health and hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: For you, I don't have the concern.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I just want to make sure it's across the board that we're all utilizing the same approach, caring for the patient and encouraging them, because this is a very challenging time where people are really scared.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks how H&H ensures language access for enrollment, scheduling, and clinical services. Long cites the 646-NYC-CARE line's telephonic interpretation in 300 languages and dialects.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about language access; Long cites 300-language line

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: New York City Care services diverse patient populations with a wide range of language needs.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What steps in New York City Health Hospital are taking to ensure members can access enrollment, appointment scheduling, care coordination, and clinical services in their preferred language?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Our 646-NYC care number allows you to, through telephonic interpretation, access 300 languages and dialects.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks whether H&H has assessed language access needs and identified gaps. Long says a team monitors wait times for interpretation, and Jimenez lists Spanish, Chinese and related dialects, French, and Polish as the most requested languages.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about language access assessments; Jimenez on top languages

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Have there been any recent assessment of language access needs among New York City Care members, and what gaps, if any, has H&H identified in interpretation or translation services?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we have a team that continually goes through wait times, things like that, to make sure that for the many languages and dialects that we interpret for, that we have reasonable wait times and good access.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I have not heard any issues recently.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I do have the most common languages that people request.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Phil, give me just a moment.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: It's Spanish, Chinese, and its related dialects, French, and Polish are the most commonly requested.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: But really at contact, we ask people, what is your preferred language?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And it's clearly visible when anyone interacts with them.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: So I always check to see, does this person prefer Spanish or French?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And then I have the...

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: A phone on my desk that at the touch of a button I can have a telephoning interpretation available so that I can communicate with the patient.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks how H&H monitors whether language barriers contribute to missed appointments or lower utilization. Long says H&H examines no-show rates by population and hasn't seen noteworthy trends, and describes MyChart scheduling.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks how H&H monitors language barriers; Long on no-show rates

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How does H&H monitor whether language barriers are contributing to missed appointment, delayed care, or lower utilization of services among New York City care members?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So the main way that we look at that is through our no-show rates, and we break it down by population and see if there are any trends that we've seen.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: This is something that we continually monitor.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I haven't seen any trends that would be noteworthy to be responsive to your question.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But we do look very carefully at how our patients are making appointments, whether they come or not, if it's based on how long the appointment was scheduled out for, if it's based on whether

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: we allow you to schedule through MyChart, so you can log on to MyChart and make your appointment with me as a new patient or existing patient directly on MyChart.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we look at the no-show rates there.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we have different ways of looking at it, and it's something we'll continue to look at going forward.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks whether H&H is seeing an increase in scared patients and whether it has enough staff to handle enrollment. Long calls the coming Medicaid changes a crisis affecting up to 900,000 New Yorkers but says it is foreseeable, unlike COVID.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks if H&H is prepared for a surge of scared patients

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Do you observe an increase of people seeking it for the health and saying that now they're scared?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Is that an increase right now?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If there's an increase, we know it's coming.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So are we prepared for it?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Do we have enough staff?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: To take care of their enrollment for like the one that coming to enroll for Medicaid or whatever that we can assess what's going on.

chapters.summary: Long describes H&H's preparation, including financial counseling teams and maximizing NYC Care capacity through a care team model with treat-to-target nurses and clinical pharmacists. He says H&H will do everything so nobody is turned away.
chapters.title: Long calls coming Medicaid changes a crisis and details preparation

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yeah, that is, in my view, this is going to be a crisis.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's going to be a crisis with up to 900,000 New Yorkers at risk for losing Medicaid.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The difference between this crisis and COVID, as you brought up earlier, though, is that we can see this coming.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we're doing many things right now to strengthen our resources to help you to stay on insurance and to strengthen the NYC Care Program.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: In terms of, just to quickly, I'll just say in a line, we're putting teams together to help you with.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Financial counseling, things like that that you would need.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And on the NYC Care side, what we're doing to get ready is to make sure that we're maximizing our capacity now.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: One of the important ways that we do that is we very carefully built a care team model so that it doesn't need to be me that sees you for every single visit that you need.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It could be our treat-to-target nurse that sees you for your blood pressure or diabetes control, which is a highly effective evidence-based program.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It could be our clinical pharmacist.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: That's visits I don't need to have with you to control your diabetes that we can have in a different way.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we are bolstering our capacity to get ready.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We are solidifying our relationships with our community partners.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We see this coming, and as always with New York City Health and Hospitals, we will do everything in our power so that nobody will ever be turned away.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks whether H&H has the resources to meet the coming demand. Long says H&H is in constant communication with OMB and expects NYC Care to expand, with coverage disruption creating fluctuating enrollment.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks if resources can meet demand; Long on OMB talks

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So do you believe that we have resources to meet the demand that's coming over our head?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So the resources for NYC Care, we are in constant communication with OMB about the money that we're spending, the money that we need both for NYC Care and for us as a system.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But we anticipate the NYC Care program is going to expand.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I think I just want to emphasize one of the things that you said earlier.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's not just going to expand in terms of people permanently enrolling in the NYC Care program.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: What I think is going to happen is you use the words coverage disruption.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I think that's going to be what happens.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So it's going to be a complicated protocol of we call you, talk to you about recertification, talk to you about work requirements, works for some people, others fall through the cracks, maybe for two months.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But in that period of time, we'll enroll you in NYC Care.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Then maybe you enroll back in Medicaid.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But it's going to be a lot of this like,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: fluctuating types of coverage that people have.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we see that coming as part of this crisis from a mile away, which is why we're making sure that we have a strong contact center, a strong financial counselor team, things like that, so that whatever happens to you, the bottom line is you'll never lose your doctor and you'll always be covered in our system.

chapters.summary: Narcisse presses for NYC Care's current enrollment capacity. Long explains that if every primary care panel were filled at 1,750 patients per provider, H&H could take in 15,000 to 20,000 patients today.
chapters.title: Narcisse presses on NYC Care enrollment capacity; Long gives 15,000-20,000 figure

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: A follow-up question for me.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Do you think, I mean, what's the capacity that actually of enrollment that you can endure right now with the resources that you have?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So today we could take in on the level of tens of thousands of new patients to New York City Health and Hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Now that's not exclusively NYC care, but that's what the teams that we have today.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So seeing that this is something that's going to be coming up on the horizon, we are seeking to do everything we can.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: To make our system strong, the program strong, and build as much capacity as we can.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But we do think that there's going to be thousands, if not tens of thousands, of New Yorkers that maybe it's not for the full year, but are going to be affected by these coverage disruptions and would benefit from enrolling in the NYC Care program going forward.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I just want to be specific.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What's the structure capacity that you have in NYC Care right now?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You don't have to be specific.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Actually, give me a range of what you can actually absorb.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Well, so the, I can be specific, but it's to a little bit of a broader question.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we look at capacity for the primary care capacity we have across New York City Health and Hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So the simple math is if I filled, remember I said earlier in my test,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: that we have a panel size of 1,750 patients per primary care doctor, per 1.0 FT, very precise.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: If we filled everybody's panel so that every panel for every primary care provider would be full, we could take in 15,000, 20,000 patients today.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So it's not infinite, it's not zero, and that's something that we're going to seek to strengthen as we go forward.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks about NYC Care's annual budget and cost per member, and whether H&H will need new city funding if enrollment climbs. Long says the program's budget is $100 million a year, unchanged for several years, covering CBO payments, marketing, member cards, and care coordination.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about NYC Care budget; Long cites $100 million

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Before I pass it on to my colleagues, there's a couple of questions, books, powers left on a budget capacity.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What is New York City Care current annual budget and cost per member?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If enrollment climbs because of federal cut, does H&H expect to need new city funding?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That's where I was going with you.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I figured.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So the budget that we have for the NYC Care Program today is $100 million a year.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: By the way, that's been the same budget that we've had since a couple of years after the inception of the program.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So within that budget, that includes things like the payments we make to our CBO partners.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It includes marketing.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It includes the cards that we talked about earlier that send you in the mail.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And it includes the coordination of care for our new patients, which need more.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: They're going to see Dr.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Jimenez or me in clinic.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So clinical services, too.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: As the program's expanded, the amount of money that we spend for the program has expanded too.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we are in very close communication with OMB about the cost of the program from our point of view, you know, stacked up against the $100 million that we're out.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks what else is needed beyond funding to support New Yorkers losing coverage. Long says the key is a unified message that health care is a human right and that calling 646-NYC-CARE unlocks enrollment and a primary care appointment.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks what else is needed; Long on the one number to call

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Beyond funding, what else is needed to make sure as many New Yorkers who are losing coverage are supported by NYC Care or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's really you.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: If we could walk out of the hearing today all believing and saying that health care is a human right and you just have to call that 10-digit number, then we will have made the world a better place.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We need everybody to let New Yorkers know that calling 646-NYC-CARE unlocks the gateway for them and their family members to enroll in insurance or in NYC Care, but not leave that phone call without an appointment to a life-saving primary care visit.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: In a time when people are terrified about Trump's policy and what this means for them and all these things, having one number to call, I think, is the most important thing we can communicate together.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm in agreement with you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm fighting you there.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I love it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Ever since started.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm going to pass it on to my colleagues out of the ball.

chapters.summary: Aldebol notes Hispanic New Yorkers are uninsured at twice the rate of Black and Asian and three times the rate of white New Yorkers, and asks about NYC Care demographics and enrollment gaps. Jimenez begins to answer.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about NYC Care demographics and enrollment gaps

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Always a pleasure to hear you speak.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I, you know, the data shows that, you know, Hispanic New Yorkers are uninsured at twice the rate of black and Asian and three times the rate of white New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What are the...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Demographics of New York City care enrollees and do you see a gap in enrollment?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Great question, Jonathan.

chapters.summary: Jimenez says 71% of NYC Care members are Hispanic or Latinx and 13% are Black or African American. He says H&H constantly looks for uninsured, unconnected residents and cites equal colon cancer screening rates across insurance types.
chapters.title: Jimenez on member demographics and equal outcomes

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: So a predominant number, a percentage of our members are Hispanic or Latinx, 71%, and 13% are black or African American.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: With respect to gaps, we are constantly looking for folks who are uninsured and unconnected to care.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: It's very hard to get a sense of what a denominator is, but in terms of how many people are out there that are uninsured and unconnected,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: which is why our mission is always to be in every place we can be, because every time I meet someone who hasn't seen a doctor in 10, 20 years, which unfortunately still happens,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: we know we have more work to do.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: The thing that gives me pride in working at New York City Health and Hospitals and doing the work we do is that we do not discriminate based on whether you're insured or have insurance.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And we see that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: in the outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: So we mentioned colon cancer screening rates, for example.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: In New York City health and hospitals, whether you have health insurance from Medicare, commercial insurance, Medicaid, or uninsured and enrolled in NYC Care, the screening rate is the same, which is

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: just a miracle that we take for granted here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: I don't take it for granted as a primary care doctor, certainly.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And we see that across the board with control for diabetes, control for hypertension.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that that was clear because we are constantly looking for where are the gaps?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Where are the populations that we need to get up to the standard of care?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And that is shown in the results that we produce.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether H&H targets particular communities where it sees gaps in insurance coverage. Long begins by crediting CBO partnerships as a cornerstone of the program's success.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks whether H&H targets communities with coverage gaps

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yeah, do you have any, do you target particular communities where you're seeing this gap in insurance coverage?

chapters.summary: Jimenez says H&H contracts with 20 community-based organizations that reflect New York City's diversity, speak dozens of languages, and operate in every borough. He says H&H meets with them monthly to share feedback and identify where to be.
chapters.title: Long and Jimenez on CBO outreach across boroughs

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Well, I'll start.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: In your outreach, I mean.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, no, totally.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I'll start and I'll turn to Jonathan.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But I want to, I think outreach is so important.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And for me, I'll say on a personal level, this program is how I really learned, you know, the value and absolute crucial role that outreach has in a program like this.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: If you take out our relationships with our CBO partners, if you take out the outreach components of the program, I don't think it would have succeeded.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So I think that from the beginning of the program, our decision to make sure that we were in partnership with CBOs, I think, has been a cornerstone of our success.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Jonathan is very close to that, so if you want to share a little more about how things have gone.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: We contract with 20.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: community-based organizations that have been serving their community for decades and are well-trusted messengers about the care that we provide and about the enrollment process.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And we strive, when we contract with them and partner with them, to make sure that they also reflect the diversity of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: So they speak dozens of languages and have served all the different communities in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: They're in every single borough.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: So that's sort of our approach to the gaps.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Let's be in as many places as possible and anywhere that we're needed.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: And we also receive feedback, important feedback, regularly from them.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: We meet with them monthly on an individual basis and then all together as well monthly to share both between them experiences about.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: Where we need to be that we aren't already, and also receive feedback about what's an event that we need to go to that we haven't been already present at.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Happy to have you at all of my events in District 13.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: A couple more questions if I may, Chair.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks about capacity at Jacobi Hospital in her Bronx district, noting the borough's 7.1% unemployment rate and concerns about Medicaid work requirements. Long agrees capacity must be built.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about Jacobi capacity and Bronx unemployment

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: How many, what's the capacity at Jacoby Hospital, which is in my district in the Bronx?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And has that number changed and do you anticipate that number changing?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And I ask that question because Bronx has the highest unemployment rate in the entire city at 7.1% right now.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And compared to...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Four or five percent in other parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And looking ahead to, you know, the employment requirements now with Medicaid, we're going to have a lot of people in the Bronx losing coverage.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And that's a great concern of mine, particularly for hospitals like Jacobi, North Central Bronx, all the public hospitals in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: We need to build capacity there.

chapters.summary: Long says New York State has applied to CMS for a work requirement exemption for the Bronx, which he believes meets the criteria but awaits approval. He says it would help in year one but H&H should build capacity and do outreach regardless.
chapters.title: Long on Bronx work requirement exemption application

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I couldn't agree more.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: As you know, I've been a primary care doctor in the Bronx for almost 10 years now.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So I am desperately worried about every single one of my patients when they come in.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I'm already thinking, you know, what's your role going to look like when you have to recertify over six months?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: What's your role going to look like when you have to go through the work requirements?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Because I know you're not working now for X, Y, and Z reasons.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: In the Bronx specifically, New York State has an application now to CMS, which I don't believe has been approved, but I think New York State's done everything they can to have the work requirement exemption for the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I believe New York State believes that the criteria are met, but I think CMS has to approve it.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: That will be– I don't want to make it seem like that's a panacea to the problem, to the issues that people in the Bronx, my patients, will have.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But it will be something that will be helpful to get our feet under us in year one, especially the program.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: From my point of view, though.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Just to agree with you, even if we get this exemption in year one that's specific to the Bronx, I don't think we should do anything else differently, though.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I think we should build capacity the same way.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Maybe we should have a little bit more time.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And I think we should do the same outreach to get people ready.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: to recertify, see what it takes, see what it feels like, see what it means for them.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And I think we should treat the work requirements in a similar way to get people ready too.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So regardless, we're going to have all the folks on the Bronx that we need.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And if we happen to get this exemption too, that would make it potentially a little bit easier for my patients.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks how patient outcomes at Jacobi compare to other H&H hospitals and what is being done to close gaps. Long says H&H can pull data from its population health dashboard.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks how Jacobi outcomes compare to other H&H hospitals

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: How do patient outcomes at Jacobi compare to other H&H hospitals, and what is being done to close any of those gaps?

chapters.summary: Long notes the Bronx often ranks last among New York's 62 counties for health outcomes, but says his Bronx clinic won an award for the best blood pressure control in the state, with an 84% hypertension control rate. He calls for working together to spread that success.
chapters.title: Long on Bronx health outcomes and hypertension control award

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Good question.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We can pull the data on the outcomes in Jacobi.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We actually have a population health dashboard, so I can pull up in a matter of minutes by site, by Gotham site, or

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: by hospital, and pull up things like A1C control for diabetes, hypertension control, things like that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I do just want to say one thing, because you and I are, I know, very close in how much we care about the health outcomes in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: As I'm sure everybody knows, the Bronx is often listed as number 62 in terms of health outcomes of the 62 counties in New York State.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But a little bit of reason to be optimistic about how we can do things differently is where I practice in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's not Jacoby, it's more Sania, so just down the street.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We recently got an award for having the best blood pressure control in all of New York State.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Beat every other place, every other private.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So even though the Bronx, on average, has lower health outcomes, we at New York City Health Hospitals and Mike

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: clinic have proven that we can exceed everybody else too.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So how can we provide that care, which I believe we do at all of our clinics, everywhere, both across health and hospitals, but across New York City as well, to regale you with a few more data points.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Our hypertension control rate in my clinic is 84%.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So between eight and nine out of every 10 of my patients that have high blood pressure, I have the certainty to know that I'm going to get them under good life-saving control.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So I care very deeply about the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We've shown in the Bronx that we could do a better job than anybody else in New York State.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So let's work together to make it happen everywhere in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Jimenez
utterances.text: You're very welcome.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: CM Feldman.

chapters.summary: Felder raises H&H's proposed absorption of financially distressed Maimonides Medical Center and asks whether it would become an NYC Care provider, the added uninsured volume and cost, and whether projections will be shared. He offers to receive answers in writing.
chapters.title: Felder questions H&H on Maimonides absorption and Medicaid rates

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: So I'm going to do the same thing that my colleague did.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I'll mention a few questions at once.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: So H&H is currently pursuing the absorption of Maimonides Medical Center.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure you're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: Which is reportedly financially distressed, and that's been one of the reasons of the change.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: H&H has made my money's future financial stability contingent on being able to collect enhanced, I underline that, Medicaid reimbursement rates.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: Hundreds of thousands of recipients in NYC, New York City, may no longer be eligible.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: NYC Care does not replace the Medicare reimbursement lost when a patient becomes uninsured.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: So the following three questions.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: Would Maimonides become an NYC care provider under the proposed takeover?

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: Two, what will be the additional uninsured patient volume and cost?

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: And does the financial plan for my modity?

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: patients moving from Medicare coverage to NYC care?

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: And finally, will you provide the council with projections showing how NYC care and hospital services at Maimonides would be protected if those payments

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: or Medicaid enrollment declines?

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I just want, I don't want to feel like I jammed you with something that really wasn't on the agenda for the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: So if you want to, you know, get me the information, you know, and give it to the chair as well, you know, in writing, you know, hopefully

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: expeditiously, I would be happy.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: If you want to answer me, I'm happy as well.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I'm just, no, I mean that seriously.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I don't want to feel like, you know, you were here, so I got you, you know, that's all.

chapters.summary: Long acknowledges the concern, noting the Maimonides financial plan relies on enhanced Medicaid rates that only work if patients stay on Medicaid. He says NYC Care is only half the equation and H&H will focus on keeping people insured, promising written follow-up.
chapters.title: Long on Maimonides financial plan and keeping patients on Medicaid

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: No, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Maybe I can answer a couple of your questions here, and then we can get back to you in writing with the rest.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yeah, sure.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Because I think you bring up a very, very legitimate concern.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Which is a lot of the basis for the health and hospitals, but also with the integration of Maimonides, the financial plan is based on the average commercial rates, which would be the enhanced Medicaid rates.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But that's only going to work if people stay on Medicaid.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So I think that is a very, very legitimate and extremely important point.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: As it pertains to what we've talked about here today in NYC Care, I think I want to emphasize one of the things I said earlier, and then we'll get back to you in writing about the rest.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: While NYC Care is very, very important and has made a tremendous difference for our patients, it's half the equation as we're seeking to fight back against all these changes coming up.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The other half is how can we keep people on the insurance plans that they were on before?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And that's where I think with the joining together of Maimonides, we have to make sure that we have plans that are very carefully curated to meet the needs of the patients of Maimonides.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The good news is, I think with what we've seen in EP5 so far in our approach with financial counselors, we've seen that we can be effective.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But it's not a done deal.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I mean, this is going to be that crisis we can see coming, you know, six months down the line here.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So you can count on us having a laser focus on keeping people on Medicaid because I couldn't agree with you more about that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And for some of the details about the process for that, how that pertains to the financial plan, things like that, we can get back to you in writing.

chapters.summary: Felder says he doesn't see how Maimonides can increase Medicaid recipients given the federal cuts, calling the situation 'kryptonite' even for a Superman. Long says he understands and will be in touch.

utterances.text: Yeah, I just want to, first of all, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I just want to repeat that as it is, the plan was to try to increase the Medicaid recipients that they're serving.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I don't see how...

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: No matter how good a job you do and anybody else does, I don't see how it's possible that

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: That's going to happen certainly not in the, you know, in the at least short term, you know.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I don't see how it's possible, you know, with the cuts.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: No matter how, you know, even if you're Superman and I, you know, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: This is kryptonite, you know.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: So I just, I certainly want the information you send me.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I'm just going to say no matter what you send me, I don't see in a practical way how the...

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I think you understood the rest.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Very much understand and appreciate, and we'll be in touch.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.text: CM Sanchez.
