chapters.summary: Narcisse asks about current wait times for primary, specialty, and behavioral health services and how they've changed. Long explains the collaborative care model for behavioral health, where social workers under a psychiatrist's supervision deliver therapy and high-acuity patients get same-day warm handoffs.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about wait times; Long on collaborative care for behavioral health

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What are the current average wait times for NYC care members to access primary?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You told me two weeks.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I can say it again.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But the specialty, the specialty, the behavioral health services, and how have those wait times changed over the last three fiscal years?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yeah, so behavioral health is a really good question.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So similar to specialty care, we don't just make referrals and create a wait list for behavioral health.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: What we do is we triage based on acuity or need.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And I'll give you a very pragmatic example of this, but I think it really points out the cornerstone of our approach.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We believe strongly in the collaborative care program and approach to behavioral health.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: For everybody, what that is, is it is a team of social workers under the supervision of one psychiatrist that can deliver therapy and care to people with depression or anxiety.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The way it works is we screen all of our patients for depression and anxiety, and then among those that screen positive, we either offer to connect you to collaborative care or, this is where the triage piece comes into it, if your PHQ-9 is high enough,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: we actually do a warm handoff to your social worker that will be your treating social worker that day.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I do that all.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And myself.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I walk my patient to, her name is Doris, sorry Doris, our social worker, that will be their collaborative care therapist.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And then that way we can assess for safety, but also get them engaged, make them comfortable with who's going to be delivering care to them going forward.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So the answer to your question of what are the wait times for behavioral health care, it depends on your acuity, depends on other factors.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But ultimately, collaborative care lets us get everybody in the door much more quickly because we're basically amplifying the reach of one psychiatrist through all the different social workers that are on that team.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And if you have enough of a need right away, we'll do a warm handoff to give you a same-day visit.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Sorry, I was not on.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks about wait times for mammograms and colonoscopies compared to prior years. Long describes same-day mammogram access that reduces wait times and no-shows, and says FIT tests have dramatically cut colonoscopy wait times by focusing colonoscopies on high-risk patients.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about screening wait times; Long on same-day mammograms and FIT tests

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay, what are the current average times for NYC care members seeking screening, mammograms, and colonoscopy, and how do those wait times compare to previous years?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So I'll start with mammograms and I'll talk about colonoscopies because that pertains to the fit test that we talked about.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: One of the things that we've started to do now, which has been proven very effective for increasing the proportion of our eligible women that receive mammograms, is offering same-day access.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So what I do for my patients is when they come and see me, if it's one of my patients that's going to need a mammogram in the coming months, I say, you're here today.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Can you take, do you have a little bit of time to stay?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And then I actually can make their appointment for them to receive their mammogram the same day that they see me.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: That's actually solved a couple of problems.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's actually reduced wait times, not only because we see a lot of people the same day, but also we were seeing a higher no-show rate because we'd schedule somebody out and then they wouldn't go, and then we'd have that slot that wasn't able to be filled.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So that enables us for patients that don't want to wait to have a sooner appointment, too, for their mammogram.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So same-day access, too.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I would say it's the most important thing we've done.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: For colorectal cancer screening, our preferred test is the FIT test, which is that once-a-year test that we do in collaboration with our nursing members of our team.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And that doesn't take very much time.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We basically, our nurses educate them on the test, give them the test.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I see this happen every week.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: And then they take the test themselves, and oftentimes they'll do it at home or in the clinic and give it right back to us.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: For those that need a colonoscopy, there had been, you mentioned from before compared to now, there had been longer wait times for colonoscopies before when we were doing screening colonoscopies on everybody.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Now we focus on the two populations that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Somebody that's had a positive test in the past or a family history.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So that's how it caused a dramatic decrease in wait times.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Like approximately?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We can get back to you on the details, but it's very significant.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks which specialties face the greatest demand and where access challenges remain. Long lists OB/GYN, eye care, dental, cardiology, and podiatry, and says neurology wait times are currently longer after losing neurologists.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks which specialties face greatest demand; Long on neurology wait times

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Which specialties currently experience the greatest demand among NYC care members, and are there service areas where access challenges remain?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So the top five areas when you go beyond primary care are OBGYN, eye care, dental, cardiology, and podiatry.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And are there service areas where access challenges, they remain throughout?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's a good question.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The reality is access challenges with different specialties change day to day.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So if we lose a team of rheumatologists or neurologists, that will cause, they'll make it harder to access services in those specialties.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So, for example, right now, we have longer wait times for neurology.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Because we lost neurologists that were in our system.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So now we're seeking to build that back up, and then when we have, the wait times will go back down, and there may be another specialty in the future if some people should leave that would have longer wait times.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So it is a moving target.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I think it, to me, though, speaks to the importance of we're not just reliant on

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: putting your name on a wait list, which was the way things have been done in the past.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Today, if you have a need, we're going to have the neurologist look at your need, for example, through the e-consult.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Maybe you don't need to be seen.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I'll give you a good example of this.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We recently had a backlog in hematology.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Hematology is an interesting field in medicine, as you know, because they rarely ever need to see the patient.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's all...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You don't see the patient.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So it can be answered via questions.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So what we did to unlock access there and really solve that problem was we put everything through eConsult, and lo and behold, what you'd expect to happen happened.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: The vast majority of hematology needs were addressed with a response back.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we have different ways of addressing needs as they change with respect to specialty access, but I want to see care patients have the same access that all of our other patients do, starting with e-consult to make sure that any of our patients with more need are seen more quickly.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay, so there is nothing you can tell me on which one is the longest in the way.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: the specialty that you have that mostly like the top one now.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We can pull the top ones today.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I just want to give the caveat that it may be different in next week, next month.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks what steps H&H is taking to address specialty capacity constraints. Long describes joining a national e-consult collaborative, workforce planning tied to residency cycles, direct access scheduling in five areas, and time-released appointment slots.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks how H&H addresses specialty capacity constraints

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So what are the steps you're taking for those to address the capacity constraint?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So a couple of things.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So in terms of specialty capacity, we have several workflows that we're working on now.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Number one is making sure that we have high quality e-consult for every specialty in every clinic.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: What we're doing for that is we actually joined a national collaborative for e-consult.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we've been able to learn the best practices from everybody across the country.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we have the metric that we're trying to hit, which is we want one out of every five e-consults.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: To be answered such that the patient doesn't need to be seen in the clinic.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We're getting close to that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We know that's the right metric to hit because others have hit that metric and we're learning from them in this national collaborative that we've joined.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's through the AAMC.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Other things that we're working on is on the workforce side, we're doing workforce planning to see where, I gave the example of neurology a minute ago,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: but where people have left our system recently or where we know we're going to have gaps in the future, and very proactively with our hiring affiliates looking for people in those specialties, which oftentimes cycle along the lines of residencies.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So it's the easiest time to hire people in July because they just finished their residency or fellowship.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So we can plan ahead in that way with workforce planning.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Other things that we're doing are with some specialties, we're trying out direct access scheduling.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So you can actually schedule an appointment through my chart.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: That's live in five areas today.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We also are looking at time release slots or optimizing templates.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So this is a little bit in the weeds, but you asked the question that has piqued my interest.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So one way that we learned in primary care, which we're now talking to our specialty councils to, is if you release an appointment a certain days ahead of when a patient would want to be seen, they're more likely to go to that appointment.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So it used to be in primary care, we'd schedule an appointment three months out, and then the no-show rate was very, very high.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It was more than 50% for new patients because nobody knows what they're going to be in three months.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So what we did is today, we're really learning from what we did with NYC Care as well, we time release appointments at 10 days.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So that's sort of the sweet spot of maximizing your chance you're actually going to go to that appointment and giving you the feeling that you're accessing care in a time frame that makes sense for you.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So now that we've done that and succeeded in primary care, we're doing that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: We're going to we're talking to our specialty colleagues about.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: optimizing their templates as well.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Other things that we're doing to increase access, so I could keep going here, I'll just give one more example, is using the contact center in different ways.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So it used to be that you would, for a lot of specialty clinics, have to call yourself, wait on hold, and also there were appointment slots that weren't taken, so it was not an efficient way of doing things.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Having one protocol where our contact center is able to actually go into the templates and schedule appointments directly, we just started to do that for the first time in behavioral health a year ago.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I believe the statistic, I'll have to fact check this, but I'm pretty sure this is right, is we've unlocked 4,000 new appointments that wouldn't have existed before.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: That's 4,000 New Yorkers that have behavioral health issues that wouldn't have been seen before if we hadn't been able to optimize our templates and have the contact center really increase our efficiency.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So I know I can keep going all day on this, so I'll conclude there and see if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yeah, you did.

chapters.title: Narcisse asks about rheumatology access; Long says it has improved

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I know from last time, I don't remember when was the last hearing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I cannot recall which hearing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Rheumatology is one of the hardest ones to get.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How are we doing with rheumatology?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Oh, you have a great memory.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It was the show hearing.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: Yes, you're exactly right.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: I gave the example then because at that point we had lost several neurologists at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So I believe we've actually rehired off to double check, but I think we filled all the vacancies.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: If not, we've made significant progress.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So rheumatology.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: So rheumatology is not the same issue today that it was when we last talked.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It's better.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: It's much better today.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Ted Long
utterances.text: But it's a perfect example to your point of specialty access changes when people leave our system and we have to then focus on hiring and using these other strategies or levers to pull that I just talked about.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
